sum: Lowe's is heading into its third-quarter earnings report with management's lower 2026 outlook putting demand and profitability at the center of the investment case. An analysis published by Earnings Whispers on Tuesday, November 10, said the November 18 report will show whether the reset was deep enough.

The company has pointed to sluggish do-it-yourself demand, a tariff-related price battle and a weaker new-home market. Those pressures have made the professional and builder-oriented parts of the business more important as Lowe's works to offset softer demand for large discretionary projects.

Management now expects full-year sales of 92 billion US dollars and adjusted earnings per share of 12.25 US dollars, according to the analysis. The outlook also implies roughly flat comparable sales, leaving investors focused on whether the retailer can stabilize demand without sacrificing margin.

The third-quarter setup is demanding. Wall Street expectations cited by Earnings Whispers call for adjusted earnings per share of 2.85 US dollars, down 6.9 percent from a year earlier, on revenue of 22.36 billion US dollars, up 7.4 percent. The combination would point to growth outside the core store base but weaker profitability, making gross margin and promotional intensity key indicators.

Gross margin declined by 80 basis points in the previous quarter as fuel and transportation costs rose. Management also said those pressures would intensify in the second half. Tariff refunds supported second-quarter adjusted earnings per share by 11 cents, but the company's second-half outlook did not assume further refunds, leaving less room for an earnings cushion.

Comparable sales have slowed over three quarters from 1.3 percent to 0.6 percent and then 0.2 percent, while customer transactions fell 2.1 percent. Against that trend, online sales growth of more than 15 percent, seven consecutive quarters of positive appliance comparable sales and continued gains in Pro and Home Services are the operating bright spots highlighted in the analysis.
The November 18 release will therefore be judged on more than headline revenue.

Kalispell police investigate flock camera vandalization at Lowe's
sum: KALISPELL, Mont. — Automated license plate readers continue to spark debate in Kalispell with residents raising concerns about privacy and surveillance. Now, that debate is raising questions about how private businesses use the technology.

The Lowe's in North Kalispell uses four Flock LPR cameras in their parking lot. The Kalispell Police Department said those cameras were vandalized on Sept. 26 and 28. Both vandalizations involved physical damage to the cameras, but police said it's unclear whether anyone was trying to remove them.
The incidents come as the city faces its own debate over license plate readers.
In August, city council voted five to two to remove funding for the technology from its upcoming budget, following public pushback over privacy concerns.

"They're already collecting all of our data on our cell phones. Everything goes to the cloud these days, you know, what more do we need? We've lost so many freedoms already, so do what's right, please, I beg of you," Kalispell resident Laura Lee O'Neil said in public comment.
But the cameras at Lowe's are separate from the city's proposed program.

Kalispell Mayor, Ryan Hunter told NBC Montana the city does not take a position on the camera vandalism at Lowe's because they are on private property. Also, Flathead County Sheriff, Brian Heino said people overall want a balance of privacy, but the laws are pretty clear; people cannot damage other people's property.

Kalispell Police investigate vandalism of Flock cameras
sum: When a photo depicting a toppled license plate reading camera in Kalispell's Hutton Ranch Plaza was posted to Facebook in September, one user offered bail money to culprit.

A month earlier, another account posted a photo showing at least two cameras and their attached solar panels covered in bright orange spray paint. Users lauded the unidentified vandal as a hero, commending the person on a job well done.
And when Kalispell City Council considered buying license plate reader technology to enforce parking, residents both in and outside of Kalispell were quick to pack city meetings in opposition.

Much of the scorn residents have expressed toward automated license plate readers in recent months mirrors criticism across the nation. Opponents often cite privacy concerns, fear of government mass surveillance and the potential for misuse by law enforcement.

The high-speed cameras capture images of license plates and store them in searchable, centralized databases. Law enforcement and private companies can use the information to track vehicle movements over time, according to digital rights group, Electronic Frontier Foundation.
Flock Safety, one of the largest manufacturers of the surveillance systems, has captured the bulk of the public's ire as the backlash to license plate readers has mounted.

THE KALISPELL Police Department is investigating two acts of vandalism — reported Sept. 26 and Sept. 28 — involving Flock cameras in the Lowe’s parking lot in North Kalispell. Shares of Lowe’s Companies (LOW) climbed 25.7% between October 6 and November 4, 2026, yet the stock still trades below the median S&P 500 company’s multiple. The stock trades at 19.3 times earnings, compared with 22.9 for the median company. This discount could mark a sound retailer on sale, or a fair price for a business with a real problem. So what does a buyer get from Lowe’s for that lower multiple?

A buyer gets a home improvement retailer whose sales are growing again. Revenue rose 8.2% over the twelve months ended July 31, 2026, following declines in each of the prior three twelve-month periods, though comparable sales grew far less in the latest quarter. Management said strong performance in Pro, Online and Home Services helped offset softer spending by do-it-yourself customers in the quarter ended July 31, 2026. Online sales grew 15.7% during that quarter.

Lowe’s also turns those sales into cash. The company generated $7.0 billion of free cash flow over the twelve months ended July 31, 2026, delivering a 5.5% yield on its market value. This cash more than covered the $2.69 billion it paid in dividends over the same twelve months. A buyer also pays 15.8% less per dollar of earnings than for the median S&P 500 company.

Lowe’s earned $2.4 billion of net income in the quarter ended July 31, 2026, the same as a year earlier, on an 8.3% increase in sales. Comparable sales rose just 0.2% for the quarter. On an August 19, 2026 call, management said discretionary DIY demand remains under pressure. Management also said the FBM and ADG acquisitions diluted its gross margin that quarter.

The longer record shows the same strain. Net income fell in each of the last two twelve-month periods, dropping to $6.64 billion in the twelve months ended July 31, 2026 from $6.93 billion two years earlier. Operating margin stood at 11.4% over the latest twelve months, below its 12.1% average across the last three twelve-month periods, which includes the latest.
The discount is to the market, not to Lowe’s own history. At the end of June in each of the last three years, Lowe’s stock traded at 18.1 to 18.6 times earnings, sitting below where it trades now.

Home Depot vs. Lowe's: Which Retail Giant Is Worth Betting On?
sum: The U.S. home improvement industry is witnessing an intensifying battle for market dominance as retail heavyweights The Home Depot, Inc. HD and Lowe's Companies, Inc. LOW compete for customer loyalty, market share and leadership in the professional contractor and do-it-yourself (DIY) segments. Home Depot remains the world's largest home improvement retailer, while Lowe's holds the second-largest position.

Both companies offer an extensive assortment of building materials, tools, appliances, home décor, and lawn and garden products through expansive store networks and digital platforms. While Home Depot leverages its scale, established contractor relationships and supply-chain capabilities to strengthen its leadership, Lowe's is expanding its professional customer business, enhancing omnichannel capabilities and refining its product assortment. With housing-market trends, renovation spending and evolving consumer preferences shaping industry dynamics, which home improvement powerhouse offers stronger investment potential? Let us find out.

Home Depot maintains its leadership in the home improvement industry, supported by 2,364 stores, extensive product offerings and strong relationships with professional contractors and DIY customers. Its competitive strength was evident as 13 of 16 merchandising departments delivered positive comparable sales (comps) in second-quarter fiscal 2026. Management highlighted continued market-share gains, with Pro customers outperforming DIY shoppers. Acquisitions of SRS Distribution and GMS further strengthen its contractor-focused capabilities.

Home Depot's strategy emphasizes product innovation, Pro engagement and omnichannel convenience. Its portfolio spans building materials, tools, appliances and home improvement essentials, featuring brands like Milwaukee. Digital comps grew 11%, supported by improved fulfillment capabilities. Its AI-powered Magic Apron enhances customer assistance, while nationwide express delivery offers fulfillment within three hours. Why Are Investors Discounting The High Cash Yield On Lowe’s Stock?
sum: Shares of Lowe’s Companies (LOW) sit about 37% below their February 2026 high. That decline has lifted the retailer’s cash yield. Free cash flow equals 7.0% of the company’s market value as of October 6, 2026, compared with 4.5% for the median S&P 500 company. This gap suggests one of two scenarios: either the stock is a bargain, or the market expects Lowe’s to generate less cash going forward. So why are investors paying so little for the cash Lowe’s produces?

Lowe’s generates nearly all its cash from a single business: home improvement retail. The segment accounted for 97% of revenue in fiscal 2025, which ended January 30, 2026. This cash production matters because it ultimately belongs to shareholders, whether the company distributes it or retains it. Once investors recognize that underlying value, the share price tends to follow.
Over the last twelve months, Lowe’s generated $9.3 billion from operations and spent $2.3 billion on capital projects. That combination left the company with $7.0 billion in free cash flow.

This cash generation has largely held steady over the past three years, despite a recent dip. Free cash flow stood at $6.6 billion three years ago and grew to $7.6 billion two years ago. The metric reached $7.7 billion a year ago before slipping to the current $7.0 billion. Through all 13 rolling twelve-month periods during that timeframe, free cash flow remained positive.

Lenders also have a claim on a portion of that cash. The company carries $38.8 billion of net debt, which equals 38.6% of its market value. When measured against the combined total of market value and debt, the resulting cash yield is 5.0%. Even with this debt load, the company’s operating profit covers its interest bill 6.4 times.

Investors may doubt the cash because profit margins have narrowed and management has lowered its forecast for the year. During the fiscal Q2 2026 earnings call on August 19, 2026, management cut its full-year sales forecast to $92 billion, the low end of its earlier range of $92 billion to $94 billion.

While total sales in the second quarter rose 8.3% from a year earlier, comparable sales grew only 0.2%. At the same time, the operating margin over the last twelve months fell to 11.4%, down from 12.4% a year ago.
